newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaitis to slowly replace expats in state jobs.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaitis to slowly replace expats in state jobs.

text.p: Kuwait is pushing ahead to gradually reduce the number of foreigners in the public sector, officials said on Wednesday.
Economists expect the plan to have limited immediate effect, pointing out that many Kuwaitis, used to high state wages, could refuse to take less prestigious jobs currently done by foreigners.
"Government institutions are acting according to plans to hire Kuwaitis instead of foreign workers," a senior official told Reuters. "Such efforts take time to be achieved."
"I cannot say I want to replace 10,000 workers this week and succeed without negative impacts," he added.

The 1996-2000 government plan calls for cutting the number of foreigners in state jobs by 10 percent every year. But officials say many Kuwaiti workers make up to three times more than a foreigner in the same grade.

More than 90 percent of Kuwaitis in the workforce are hired by the state, which spends two-thirds of its annual oil revenue on wages -- over 1.25 billion dinars ($4.18 billion) -- in the cradle-to-grave welfare state of 720,000 Kuwaitis.
Some 40 percent of the 250,000 public sector workers are foreigners, mainly Arabs and Asians. They also hold 98.6 percent of 616,000 private sector jobs, which are not attractive for Kuwaitis.
For the next school year, the Education Ministry plans to replace a few hundred foreign teachers with Kuwaitis, undersecretary Musaed al-Haroun told Reuters.
In recent months, Kuwait's ports authority made 750 foreign workers redundant, although they have not been replaced. The oil-rich Gulf Arab state has a foreign population of 1.2 million.

The state says there are less than 4,000 unemployed Kuwaitis. It has plans to train Kuwaiti state workers to make them more employable in the private sector, possibly including subsidising their salaries for several years.
"The government has set the expectations of Kuwaitis high," an economist said.
